## TL;DR

Closed the cross-process ownership race in remote validation container reaping. The old sequence made a decision from one server process's cached host-lock view, inspected a Docker container, then removed it by ID. A different RepoOS process could acquire a host slot between those actions, or begin its run while the reaper was progressing through its separate SSH commands. The reaper could therefore remove a quiet container belonging to an active validation. The fix moves the final ownership boundary onto the runner: validation slot creation and reaper admission now serialize through one atomic directory gate. A reaper transaction takes a lease only while no host slots exist; host validation commands wait while that lease is held. The lease remains through the final Docker name/state/activity checks and removal. The remote validation guide now documents this protocol.

## Work and rationale

The most recent review identified that the earlier safeguards did not establish cross-process ownership. The 40-minute lock-wait-plus-run bound and five-minute margin make old containers good candidates, and local `liveContainerNames` prevents this process from cleaning up its own work. Neither fact proves another process is not using the container. A second `docker inspect` narrows the timing window but leaves a classic check-then-act race.

I addressed the whole shared boundary rather than adding another cached lock lookup. `hostLockShell` now acquires `$LOCKROOT/.acquire-gate` immediately before examining occupied slots and creating a slot directory. While it owns that short gate, it checks for `$LOCKROOT/.reaping`; if present, it releases the gate and waits. This keeps the existing host-wide slot accounting intact while giving the reaper a synchronization point that all new validations observe.

The final `reaperRemoveCommand` transaction acquires that same gate, confirms there are no numeric slot directories, then creates `.reaping` before releasing the gate. This ordering handles both race directions: if a validation gets the gate first, the reaper sees its slot and exits without removal; if the reaper gets the gate first, a validation sees the lease and cannot create a slot until cleanup ends. The reaper then verifies the container still has the exact validation prefix, obtains fresh Docker state, checks for recent output, and runs `docker rm -f` while the lease remains held. An exit/signal trap removes only a lease this command successfully created. A busy-host or recent-output result leaves the container in place.

The process-local pool checks remain useful for avoiding unnecessary cleanup attempts and for keeping dispatch local to the reaper quiet period, but no longer claim to be the cross-process safety mechanism. `docs/remote-validation.md` now describes the host-side lease and removes the previous statement that cross-process ownership was merely best-effort.

Tests assert the generated validation lock script uses the gate and honors the reaper lease, and that the removal transaction takes the lease and performs fresh Docker inspection before removal. The existing scheduled-reaper test continues to cover both quiet and recently active candidates, including that recent activity prevents the remove command. The final requested `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed. Remote validation passed on thinkpad, including the changed-path test suite; the local format, lint, build, static guards, rendered contrast audit, and UI smoke stages also passed. One initial run stopped at formatting, so I ran `bun run fmt` and repeated the check against the formatted tree before recording this result.

## Approaches tried

The earlier implementation's candidate-age bound, process-local ownership set, and pre-removal Docker inspection were retained as filters, but review showed they could not resolve the race across processes. Simply refreshing the host lock immediately before `docker rm` would still allow a validation to acquire a slot in the gap after the refresh. Rechecking container age/activity at removal time alone would have the same flaw for a quiet run. I therefore coordinated both slot acquisition and reaper admission on the host itself. The gate is held only for the short slot allocation or lease-establishment operation; the reaper lease, rather than the gate, spans Docker inspection and removal, so ordinary slot contenders do not hold the gate while waiting for the reaper.

## Challenges and blockers

The hard part was avoiding a non-atomic sequence while preserving the existing counting semaphore and its multi-slot behavior. The gate must cover both the no-active-slot check and creation of the reaper lease; otherwise a runner could enter after the check but before lease creation. Conversely, host lock acquisition must check the lease and create its slot while holding the same gate. The removal command uses the same `$HOME/.repoos-validate-locks` root as `hostLockShell`, so processes launched by separate RepoOS servers on the same runner coordinate. This does not unify different SSH users' home directories; the existing lock protocol documents that separate users still have separate namespaces.

No live runner was exercised in this session, so no claim is made about a specific device or remote execution. The proof here is the shared shell protocol plus the passing automated repository checks. No live-runner behavior beyond this observed validation result is claimed.

## Key learnings

A cached ownership snapshot is useful for scheduling and user visibility, but it cannot authorize destructive cleanup when another process can claim ownership independently. Safety-sensitive cleanup needs a host-side lease at the same boundary used to create ownership. The key invariant is now explicit: while `.reaping` exists, no new validation slot can be created; `.reaping` is created only under the acquisition gate after confirming all slot directories are absent; and removal happens before releasing that lease. This pattern should guide future remote cleanup work that races with independently launched server processes.
